draft.title: The quadratic formula and the discriminant
card: For a quadratic \(ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\), the solutions are \(x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a}\). Write the equation with zero on one side first, then read off \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) with their signs.
Solve \(x^{2} - 2x - 15 = 0\). Here \(a = 1\), \(b = -2\), \(c = -15\). So \(x = \frac{2 \pm \sqrt{4 + 60}}{2}\), which is \(\frac{2 \pm 8}{2}\). The solutions are \(x = 5\) and \(x = -3\).
The part under the root, \(\Delta = b^{2} - 4ac\), is called the discriminant. It is worked out before the rest of the formula.
If \(\Delta > 0\), there are two real solutions. If \(\Delta = 0\), there is one. If \(\Delta < 0\), there are none, because a negative number has no real square root.
draft.remember: Find \(\Delta = b^{2} - 4ac\) first: positive gives two real solutions, zero gives one, negative gives none.

a.q: What is the discriminant of \(2x^{2} - 3x + 5 = 0\), and how many real solutions does it have?
a.why: Here \(a = 2\), \(b = -3\), \(c = 5\), so \(\Delta = 9 - 40 = -31\). It is negative, so there are no real solutions. The value 49 comes from adding 40 instead of subtracting it.
a.clue: Subtract \(4ac\) from \(b^{2}\), and square \(-3\) as a positive.

b.q: For which value of \(k\) does \(x^{2} + 6x + k = 0\) have exactly one real solution?
b.why: One solution needs \(\Delta = 0\). So \(36 - 4k = 0\), which gives \(k = 9\). The value 36 is \(b^{2}\) alone, and 3 is half of \(b\), but neither makes \(\Delta\) zero.
b.clue: Set \(b^{2} - 4ac\) equal to zero and solve for \(k\).
